archetype.name: Fringe Contender (offense-first)
archetype.definition: A 6-2 team whose efficiency profile is closer to league average: a top-seven offense and elite special teams carry a defense that ranks near the bottom in EPA allowed, and close wins have filled in the rest.

report.headline: A 6-2 record built on Goff's passing, special teams and close-game wins
report.take:
Detroit's record says contender. Its play says something more modest. The Lions are 6-2 with a point differential that ranks 10th, but their net EPA sits 16th, almost exactly league average. Two lines explain the gap. The offense is legitimately good, 7th in EPA per play and 3rd in success rate, with the passing game 4th. The defense is 30th in EPA allowed and 27th against the pass. That split isn't new: the 2022 team ranked 31st in defensive EPA and 2023 ranked 21st. Only the 2024 group paired this kind of offense with a top-10 defense, and that was the 15-win version.

The record has had help. Detroit has won 80% of its one-score games (3rd), special teams are adding 4.23 EPA a game (3rd), and it sits 0.89 wins above what the point differential implies, which itself implies about five wins. None of that is a mirage, because the Lions have also beaten the teams they were supposed to beat. But a team that wins by margins this thin with a bottom-three defense is living closer to .500 than the standings suggest. It also plays in a division where all four teams have six or more wins.

The shape of the season has changed. The first month was a shootout run: Goff throwing for 412 yards in a loss at Carolina, the defense giving up 410 through the air to New Orleans, and totals cleared routinely. The last three games were grinders: 20-17, 19-15 and 19-9. The defense looked better because Minnesota (31st offense) and Miami (26th) can't move the ball. The passing offense produced negative EPA in both of the last two games, including the Minnesota game where Detroit ran for 230 yards and threw for 176. The pass rush is real, with 27 sacks (2nd) and a QB hit rate 5th. The coverage behind it is not, and the TE1 leak, 31st in EPA per play allowed, is a weakness opponents can plan around.

Where it goes depends on whether the passing game snaps back and how quickly the secondary and linebacker room heal. Jack Campbell, a 97%-snap linebacker, is on IR until early December. D.J. Reed, a 94%-snap corner, has been out, and Kerby Joseph hasn't played at all. Four of the final eight are division games, including two against 7-2 Chicago. This is a playoff-caliber offense attached to a defense that will lose shootouts to good quarterbacks.

strengths.title: Efficient, Goff-led passing offense
strengths.body: Detroit is 4th in pass EPA and 3rd in overall success rate, and the line has allowed pressure on just 17.1% of dropbacks (5th). St. Brown's 86 targets anchor a spread-out tree that includes LaPorta, Williams and Gibbs as a receiver. History says this is durable: the offense has ranked in the top nine in EPA every year since 2022, so the last two flat passing games look more like a dip than a collapse.

strengths.title: A pass rush that finishes
strengths.body: With 27 sacks (2nd) and a QB hit rate 5th, Detroit gets home even though its pressure rate is only 9th. That suggests quick wins rather than volume, and the defense also tackles cleanly, ranking 1st in missed-tackle rate. The rush is the defense's one reliable weapon and the main reason its points allowed sit mid-pack despite the EPA.

strengths.title: Special teams tilting field position
strengths.body: At 4.23 EPA per game, special teams rank 3rd and quietly cover for some of the defense's failures. Every fourth down has been a go (1st), so Campbell is squeezing extra possessions out of the margins. The aggressiveness is a stable trait. Special-teams EPA at this level tends to swing more from week to week.

concerns.title: Coverage is a bottom-tier unit
concerns.body: Detroit is 27th in pass EPA allowed, 28th in explosive pass rate allowed and 28th on short passes, and offenses lean into it: its pass rate over norm ranks 2nd as a pass funnel. Tight ends feast, at 0.69 EPA per target allowed (31st). With Reed and Joseph missing and Campbell on IR, this is a real flaw made worse by injuries, not noise.

concerns.title: Record ahead of the efficiency
concerns.body: An 80% one-score win rate, a point differential implying about five wins and a net EPA ranked 16th all point the same way: Detroit is winning more than its play-for-play level suggests. The 2025 team ran the other way in close games and finished 9-8 with similar efficiency. Expect some give-back.

concerns.title: Stalls on third down and short yardage
concerns.body: The defense allows a 44.4% conversion rate on third down (27th) and a 66.7% touchdown rate in the red zone (22nd), which keeps drives alive. On offense, a 24.2% stuff rate (27th) and 53.3% short-yardage conversion (27th) undercut a run game that is otherwise efficient. Both trace to line-of-scrimmage play in leverage spots, and both cost points in close games.

trend.note: The early weeks were high-scoring shootouts with the defense leaking yards. The last three were low-scoring wins, with the passing offense producing negative EPA against Minnesota and Miami, a better defensive look that came against weak offenses.

nextGame.headline: St. Brown against a soft WR1 defense, Maye against Detroit's coverage
nextGame.body:
New England comes in 5-4 with a profile much like Detroit's: a top-10 passing offense under Drake Maye, who has started every game, and a defense that is 24th against the pass and 28th on deep balls. The Patriots are also 31st in turnover differential, minus 1.2 a game. The matchup is shaped by where each defense breaks. New England has been gashed by opposing WR1s, at 0.83 EPA per target (32nd), and WR2s (31st), but it smothers tight ends (3rd) and lead backs. That points the ball toward St. Brown and Williams rather than LaPorta or Gibbs. Detroit's leaky coverage faces a quarterback who holds the ball 3.16 seconds (2nd longest), which gives the Lions' rush time to get there and Maye time to find holes. The Book has Detroit by 2.5 with a 51.5 total.

Availability cuts both ways. Detroit is without Jack Campbell (97% snaps) on IR. D.J. Reed (94%), Kerby Joseph, DJ Wonnum and center Cade Mays all carry return estimates for this game date, so how many of them actually suit up shapes the back seven. New England's A.J. Brown (70% snaps) is listed out. Left tackle Will Campbell (90%) and corner Carlton Davis are questionable, center Ben Brown is doubtful, and the backfield is thin, with TreVeyon Henderson out and Rhamondre Stevenson's knee possibly costing him time. A depleted Patriots line facing Detroit's sack production is the biggest availability swing in the game.

waysToWin.title: Feed St. Brown against a WR1 leak
waysToWin.body: New England's defense has allowed the most EPA per target to opposing WR1s, and St. Brown commands Detroit's biggest target share. If Goff's passing efficiency returns to its early-season level, the Lions can win this without the run game. The Patriots' deep-ball defense ranks 28th, so Williams has room too.

waysToWin.title: Sack Maye behind a banged-up line
waysToWin.body: Maye holds the ball longer than almost anyone, and Detroit converts pressure into sacks at an elite rate. If Will Campbell sits and Ben Brown can't go, the Lions' rush can wreck drives and protect a secondary that can't win in long coverage reps.

waysToWin.title: Win the turnover battle
waysToWin.body: New England gives the ball away more than nearly any team, at 31st in turnover differential, while Detroit sits 10th. A takeaway or two hands a field-position edge to an offense and special teams that both rank among the league's best.

waysToLose.title: Maye picks apart a thin secondary
waysToLose.body: New England's passing offense ranks 9th in EPA, and Detroit's pass defense is 27th, with its best linebacker on IR and Reed and Joseph uncertain. If the rush doesn't get home, a quarterback who extends plays will find the soft spots underneath. Detroit ranks 28th on short passes allowed.

waysToLose.title: The passing slump continues
waysToLose.body: Goff's passing produced negative EPA against Minnesota and Miami, and New England's sack rate ranks 5th. If Detroit leans on a run game that gets stuffed often, and New England shuts down lead backs, drives stall into field goals in a game the total says needs touchdowns.

waysToLose.title: Third downs extend Patriot drives
waysToLose.body: Detroit's defense allows conversions on 44.4% of third downs and touchdowns on two-thirds of red-zone trips. In a near pick'em, a couple of extended drives that finish in the end zone flip a one-score game the Lions have usually won.

nextGame.watch: Whether Detroit's pass rush beats a patched Patriots line before Maye, who holds the ball 3.16 seconds, can find holes in a depleted secondary.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense is the sustainable piece. Its passing efficiency and success rate match a multi-year track record, and the last two flat games came against Minnesota's 1st-ranked defense and a road trip to Miami. The record is less sturdy. The close-game win rate and special-teams edge will likely regress somewhat, and the defense has no history of fixing itself midseason outside 2024. Campbell's return in December helps, and the secondary should be healthier soon if the estimates hold.

The schedule is split. Tampa Bay, Atlanta and Tennessee are winnable, though Tampa's defense ranks 2nd. Two games against Chicago, a trip to Minnesota's top defense and the finale at Green Bay will decide the division. Expect Detroit to keep scoring in the high 20s at home and to look mortal in the cold-weather division road games. Somewhere around 11 wins is the likeliest landing spot, with the division title a coin flip at best.
swingFactors: Health of Reed, Joseph and Campbell in the back seven
Close-game luck in four division games

confidence.note: Eight games, a clear offense-defense split, heavy defensive injuries
